**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to stay in school. In 2014 he said flatly, "Do not start a startup in college." The one exception is a side project that's already taking off on its own, and even then he only goes as far as "maybe it's reasonable to run with it." Having an idea isn't enough. Dropping out makes sense only once real users are pulling the project forward.

**Based on:** something he said. He spoke to this exact case in 2014 and came back to it in a 2026 essay.

**Why he'd say it**
- **You can't be a founder and a student at once.** "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." ([2014 Stanford lecture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1102s) @ 18:22). He said the same in 2026: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **20 is the wrong age, and waiting costs you nothing.** "20 is not the optimal time to do it." and "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." ([lecture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s) @ 18:56, @ 21:12)
- **College is for learning powerful things.** "If you wanna start a startup, what you should do in college is learn powerful things." His advice for young would-be founders comes down to two words: "just learn." (@ 30:15, @ 30:49). In 2026 he says the hard part of startups is product, and the knowledge for that comes from fields like CS or molecular biology. He still says to study CS even with AI writing code ([essay](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)).
- **The exception.** If a side project takes off: "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." (@ 21:12). In 2026 he points out that Microsoft and Meta both "got started during reading period at Harvard". For a student whose project takes off, it's "either that or drop out." ([essay](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))

**How this applies to you:** "I have an idea" is not the same as "my side project is taking off." So build it as a side project now, while you're in school. That's the path he describes, and it costs you nothing. Revisit dropping out only if users are adopting it faster than you can keep up as a student.

**Where his view shifted:** In 2026 he wrote to universities, not students, and he put more weight on the side-project route than in 2014. He wants students to have more free time for their own projects. He doesn't say whether the student should then drop out, only that they'd have to choose. His underlying rule hasn't changed: being a student and running a startup don't mix.

**One more thing:** In the same 2014 talk he says "the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it" (@ 33:36). That was aimed at people taking a job first. In the same talk he still says not to do it in college, and his line for people who are just unsure is "the only way to find out is to try, just not now." (@ 23:58)

**What would change his answer:** traction. If real users are adopting the thing on their own, you're in his exception, and dropping out becomes "maybe reasonable."

The vault has a matching note on this at `vaults/yc/wiki/founders/becoming-a-founder/should-i-start-a-startup-in-college.md`. I can save this answer to `derived/` if you want to keep it.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to keep building on the money you have, but not to wait for revenue as such. The thing to wait for is a milestone that convinces investors, usually users who love the product and a growth graph to show it. Once you have that, raise quickly, because now investors want in. If you don't have it yet, raising now mostly means a long pitch process that you'll lose.

**Based on:** mostly things he said in the vault, plus one labelled point from outside it

**Why he'd say it**
- **You can start on little money.** In 2026 he said: "I think you can still start a startup on not much money." The method is to "adjust for how much money you've got" ([PG interview, Sep 2026 @ 11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s)).
- **Raise once you hit a milestone.** "So you just do what you can on the money you got. As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more." He also said: "You're always able to raise another round, right?" ([@ 12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s))
- **Doing well is what persuades investors, not pitching skill.** "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning ... growing fast, and then simply tell investors so" ([Stanford CS183B, 2014 @ 9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s)). And: "Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money" ([@ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s)).
- **Payment is a signal, but low prices are fine early.** He advises selling "as cheaply as they need to at first; get all the users, then worry about your margins". He also warns that if you give away too much, "you lose the signal that customers send by paying you" ([*powerful*, Sep 2026](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)). So revenue matters as evidence that people want the product. It isn't the bar for raising.
- **Not in the vault:** his essays *Ramen Profitable* (2009) and *Default Alive or Default Dead* (2015) make the same case from the bootstrapping side. Earning enough to cover the founders' basic living costs means you don't need investors, and that makes it much easier to get them on good terms.

**What YC partners have seen:** Michael Seibel spent about eight months trying to raise for Justin.tv. With two months of runway left, the team switched to making the company profitable, and he says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of pitching ([YC podcast, Oct 2026 @ 6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s)). Seibel also says investors told him they chase 80–90% of the deals they do. The goal is to become a company they chase ([@ 10:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s)). The vault notes that Caldwell credits the growth-over-pitching idea to PG, so this backs up PG's view rather than independently confirming it.

**What would change his answer:**
- **The milestone needs capital.** For something like a rocket company, his answer is still to raise in stages: design and simulate on what you have, then raise enough for the next stage.
- **You're a known expert.** His example is the Starcloud founder, who raised on a white paper and a booked launch. Someone like that "comes with automatic cred" and can raise earlier.

**Caveat:** the vault notes that PG is YC's co-founder, so he has a stake in the funded-startup path. Even so, his advice here is to build leverage first, not to pitch early.

If you tell me where you are now (users, growth, burn, runway), I can apply this to your case. I can also save this answer to the vault's `derived/` folder if you want to keep it.

**Verdict:** Move to San Francisco, at least for a while. Paul Graham says this flatly: every field has one center, and for startups it's Silicon Valley. He's fine with you going back to Berlin later, but he thinks you should go.

**Based on:** said it. He was asked almost exactly this by a non-US audience in a talk in Stockholm in April 2026 ([talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8)). Berlin wasn't the city, but the question was the same. Everything quoted below is from that talk.

**Why he'd say it**
- **His answer to "should I go?" is yes.** "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([@ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s))
- **The people around you.** "You get the best peers… The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." ([@ 1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s)) He also values chance meetings: "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." ([@ 3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s))
- **It changes you.** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([@ 8:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s)) Once you see the big names up close, the goal "no longer seems an impossible goal, just a hard one." ([@ 10:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=634s))
- **Fundraising.** He says Valley investors decide faster because they compete with each other. He also says "Investors outside Silicon Valley implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate… It's the same everywhere," and that leaving for the Valley makes "this rule operate in reverse. You automatically rise in investors' opinion." ([@ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s)) That includes investors in Berlin.
- **Help from strangers.** "In Silicon Valley, people help you for no reason." ([@ 12:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=735s))
- **How he'd do it.** "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC." ([@ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s)) He admits this "will sound like I'm talking my own book."

**What he's done:** YC used to fly startups from its Boston batches to the Valley for a second Demo Day, because Boston investors wouldn't fund them. That's how Dropbox met Sequoia in 2007.

**What would change his answer:**
- **Going home is a real option, but it costs something.** He says YC startups that go home are "only about half as likely to become unicorns." He discounts that number himself: some of it is selection bias (the more determined founders stay), and Bay Area valuations are higher anyway. ([@ 18:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s))
- **Family.** "Money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company." ([@ 19:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1170s)) A Berlin founder with family ties there could reasonably go and then come back.
- **Building Berlin's scene.** He told the Stockholm audience that founders who go and come back are the best way to grow a hub at home. He said the "Silicon Valley of Europe" job "is still up for grabs," and that "All you need is a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them." ([@ 20:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1204s)) Even so, his route to building Berlin starts with going to the Valley first.

**Sam Altman (also in the vault) agrees, less firmly:** in July 2026 he said YC's rule that founders should move to San Francisco was clearly right. He thinks it's probably still good advice, but says he has less of an intuition for it now.

**Bias to note:** PG founded YC, and YC profits from founders coming to the Valley. He says so himself in the talk.

**Verdict:** PG wouldn't take your side just because you want to keep going. He'd tell you to keep the goal and give up the approach if the evidence is against it. If your co-founder's pivot keeps the same users and problem and changes only the product, he'd probably side with them. If it means dropping the problem itself, you're entitled to resist.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. He hasn't written about co-founders disagreeing over a pivot, but his essay "The Right Kind of Stubborn" (2024) gives a clear rule for deciding.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Ask what you're attached to.** "The persistent are attached to the goal. The obstinate are attached to their ideas about how to reach it." ([The Right Kind of Stubborn](https://paulgraham.com/persistence.html)) Persistent founders hold firm on decisions near the top: which problem, which users. They change the decisions lower down when the evidence turns. So work out which of those your co-founder's pivot changes.
- **Changing your mind is part of persisting.** "Resilience means setbacks can't change your morale, not that they can't change your mind. … Indeed, persistence often requires that one change one's mind." Wanting to keep going is good. Wanting to keep going *with the current approach* is not the same thing.
- **His test applies to you right now.** How do you react when someone points out a problem? The Collisons "not only listen, but listen with an almost predatory intensity," and successful people are "never more engaged than when you disagree with them." The obstinate "won't listen." Your co-founder disagreeing is the moment he'd watch.
- **Being obstinate makes hard problems harder.** "The further someone is toward the obstinate end of the continuum, the less likely they are to succeed in solving hard problems." He also says "The optimal amount of obstinacy is not zero." A little of it keeps you from panicking and pivoting at the first bad week.
- **Look at what users are doing.** In "Making Startups Powerful" (Sept 2026) he says "don't be annoyed that your users are using your product wrong; listen for the message they're sending." His example is PayPal, which started as a demo and became a payments company because users pushed it there ([source](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)). If the pivot follows real user behavior, he'd back it.
- **Michael Seibel (YC, 2019) says the same about products:** "hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely" ([video @ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s)). He warns against falling in love with your MVP.

**A way to settle it with your co-founder**
1. Write down the goal: which users, which problem. Do you both still agree on it?
2. If you do, the pivot is only about approach. Decide it on evidence about expected value: usage, retention, what users ask for. Don't decide it on who feels more strongly.
3. If the pivot drops the goal, PG says "It's ok to be irrational near the top of the decision tree." Caring about a problem others don't can mean you've noticed something they haven't. Then the question is whether you two still share a goal, and that's a co-founder problem more than a strategy problem.

**What would change his answer:** if the current approach is working (users are growing and coming back) and the pivot is driven by boredom or fear, then holding steady is persistence, not obstinacy.

One limit: the vault has nothing from PG on co-founders who disagree about direction. The YC material on co-founder conflict comes from Seibel and Dalton Caldwell. Their point is that these fights usually come from a lack of mutual respect, not from the strategy question.

**Verdict:** Ship the tiny version this week. PG would see spending months on a full-featured product before anyone uses it as the standard mistake. You learn what to build by watching real users, and growth from a small group of happy users is the signal he cares about.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has no PG quote that says "launch before it's full-featured." The blunt version of that rule comes from YC partners Michael Seibel and Dalton Caldwell. PG's own statements in the vault point the same way.

**Why he'd say it**
- **He thinks founders are already too slow, and AI hasn't fixed that.** In September 2026 he said: "we have all these powerful AI tools and there's still a lot of startups in this batch that are not shipping fast enough." ([interview @ 16:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=964s)). In the same interview he said "so far almost everything is exactly the same" about how startups work, AI included (@ 16:38).
- **Growth rate is the first thing he asks about, and it starts from a few users.** "If you pay a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers, ideally you'll kick off exponential growth by word of mouth." ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). He also says growth rate "shows whether they've built the right thing." You can't measure that until something is live.
- **Get users first and tidy up later.** "I generally advise startups to sell as cheaply as they need to at first; get all the users, then worry about your margins." ([Making Startups Powerful](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)). The order is the same as in the launch question: users first, polish second.
- **What YC as a whole says, in its partners' words, not PG's:**
  - Seibel: "if you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." He calls this "part of the YC ethos from the very beginning" ([2019 talk @ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)).
  - Seibel also redefines a launch as the point "when you get any customers," so a press launch can wait (@ 10:07).
  - In 2026 Caldwell said the "full-featured" urge is now the bigger risk. To launch his own product he "had to delete 80% of the features that I built in the MVP," and only after that did users sign up on the spot ([video @ 1:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=66s)).

**Beyond the vault:** PG's essays make this point directly, for example "Release Early, Release Often" and "Do Things That Don't Scale." They aren't in this vault yet, so I haven't quoted them.

**What would change his answer:** the only exception in the vault is Seibel's. Heavily regulated or hard-tech startups, such as insurance, banking or rockets, may not be able to launch this fast. Even then, PG's advice is to "do what you can on the money you got" and reach a milestone ([interview @ 12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s)).

The vault lacks PG's own launch essays. To make this answer rest on "said it", I can add "Release Early, Release Often" and "Do Things That Don't Scale" as sources and compile them.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you to start the startup now and skip the Google job. "Work somewhere first to learn" is advice he used to give. He has said publicly that it was a mistake.

**Based on:** something he said. He addressed this exact question in 2014 and repeated the view in 2026.

**Why he'd say it**

- **He gave your plan as advice and then took it back.** "One of the things I got wrong early on, is that I advised people who were interested in starting a startup to go work for some other company for a few years before starting their own. But, honestly, the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try and start it. You may not be successful, but you'll learn faster if you just do it." ([Before the Startup, Stanford 2014 @ 33:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2016s))
- **His view hasn't changed since.** In his 2026 essay: "The only way to learn how to start a startup is to do it." ([How Universities Should Prepare Founders](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html))
- **The skills you'd get at Google aren't the ones that matter early.** He says the hard part of a startup is product, "knowing what to build, and being able to build it". That knowledge comes from fields like computer science, "not management or finance" (same essay). He dismisses business school for the same reason: it was "designed to train the officer corps of large companies." Applying that to Google is my inference, not something he said about Google.
- **Take risks while you're young.** "The solution is to take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early." Work that eats huge amounts of time and energy is best done "when you're young and don't yet have children." ([Superlinear Returns, 2023](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)) A few years at Google uses up some of those years and gives you fewer attempts.

**What would change his answer**

- **If you're still a student.** He says "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." His advice there is to learn powerful things and work on side projects, not to take a job.
- **If you're not sure you want a high-variance life.** "Exposing oneself to superlinear returns is not for everyone. Most people will be better off as part of the pool." His test is whether you're ambitious and either very good or young enough to try and find out. If you're neither, a job is fine.
- **Michael Seibel and Dalton Caldwell (YC partners, 2026) give a narrower reason to take a job first.** If you can't come up with an ambitious idea, Seibel says: "If you're concerned by your level of mission, go work some place with high ambition." ([Low Ambition is Killing Your Startup @ 19:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=1177s)) Their reason is to raise your ambition, not to learn how startups work. So it only applies if you have no idea worth working on.

**A caveat:** Graham co-founded YC, and its model depends on people starting companies young rather than spending years at big companies first, so his view is not neutral.

**Verdict:** PG would tell you to work on the hard, ambitious idea, as long as it's the thing you're most interested in and you want a big outcome. He'd say the AI tool that makes money now is the "midwit" choice: sensible if you just want decent income, and wrong if you're young, technical and aiming high.

**Based on:** mostly what he said. He gives a rule for deciding rather than a flat answer. His view that the money-now option is incremental follows from his principles.

**Why he'd say it**
- **His rule depends on what you want.** "if your main goal is to make money, you can't usually afford to work on what interests you the most. People pay you for doing what they want, not what you want." But "if you want to become super rich, and you're young and good at technology, working on what you're most interested in becomes a good idea again." He calls this "something like a midwit peak for making money." If you want to do great work, the answer is simply yes. ([*When To Do What You Love*](https://paulgraham.com/when.html), 2024)
- **Optimizing for money gives small gains.** His office-hours question is "what would make this company more powerful?" because "Asking how the company could make more money is a good heuristic too, but it tends to yield incremental improvements." He also says early startups often pick the smaller idea out of fear: "The company is unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than they could." ([*Making Startups Powerful*](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html), 2026)
- **"Might take years" is normal.** He says founders "put your head down and work on the model train set for 10 years," and the money "takes people by surprise when it happens." What keeps them going is ambition, because "being dutiful is not enough." ([interview, Sept 2026 @ 6:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=398s))
- **Outcomes are winner-take-most.** "If your product is only half as good as your competitor's, you don't get half as many customers. You get no customers." ([*Superlinear Returns*](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html), 2023) A me-too AI tool in a crowded market is exactly where that bites.
- **The hard idea doesn't need a big budget to start.** "even a rocket startup you can start on not much money because what you do is you adjust for how much money you've got." Get to a milestone, then raise for the next stage. ([interview @ 11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s))
- **If you can't decide, you probably don't know enough yet.** "When you can't decide which path to take, it's almost always due to ignorance." The fix is to start working on the thing that interests you now, in whatever form you can. Watch out for picking work mainly for the pay, because "you'll be surrounded by other people who chose it for the same reason." (*When To Do What You Love*)

**What would change his answer:**
- **You need money soon or only want a comfortable income.** Then his rule flips and the tool that pays is fine.
- **The ambitious idea doesn't really grip you.** He says "ambitious curiosity" can't be faked, and you'd quit when it gets hard.
- **Your interests happen to be what people pay for.** Then he'd say you don't have to choose ("The odds are better when you have strange tastes").

**Other YC voices:** Seibel and Caldwell (2026) are blunter: "there aren't a lot of venture funded small businesses that make anyone any money." They limit this to venture-backed companies, though, and both are VCs. Altman says AI coding tools should push founders toward more ambitious companies, but he runs OpenAI, so he isn't neutral.

**Not in the vault:** PG's older essays *Frighteningly Ambitious Startup Ideas* and *Ramen Profitable* aren't in it. The second suggests a middle path: make just enough money to survive while you work on the big idea. That's my extrapolation from his other work, not something cited here.

**Verdict:** Build. Making something people want comes first, and an online presence isn't a substitute for it. Keep writing, though, because for PG writing is a way of thinking. Essays that sharpen your ideas are worth the time. Posting for its own sake is not.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has no PG statement about whether founders should blog. His views on startups and on writing settle it anyway.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Focus on the product.** PG warns about "playing house", where founders go through the motions of a startup and neglect "the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want" ([talk, 2014 @ 7:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=452s)). Also: "you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extend that you do" (@ 12:43). If posting online takes time from users and product, it's playing house.
- **Tricks matter far less than the real problem.** "There are tricks in the startups... But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem" (@ 13:17). Building an audience before you have a product falls in the tricks category.
- **Write anyway, but to think.** "writing is thinking. In fact there's a kind of thinking that can only be done by writing" ([Writes and Write-Nots, 2024](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html)). And: "There will still be smart people, but only those who choose to be." So writing out your strategy, your users' problem or your pitch has real value, even if nobody else reads it.
- **Writing well checks your ideas.** "something that seems clumsily written will usually have gotten the ideas wrong too" ([Good Writing, 2025](https://paulgraham.com/goodwriting.html)). If you can't write your thesis clearly, you probably haven't worked it out yet.
- **An audience can compound.** In *Superlinear Returns* he lists "growing an audience or brand" as work that compounds directly, where doing well in one cycle helps the next ([2023](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). That makes an audience a real asset over the long run. It still ranks behind having something worth talking about.

**Other YC partners (not PG):** Caldwell and Seibel (Oct 2026) say press does little for a startup ("it is shocking how little um getting press helps a startup", [@ 20:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=1228s)). As the vault summarizes them, they'd rather founders post their own content constantly, since that builds the same skills as fundraising and recruiting and gives a direct channel to users. That supports posting about real progress. It doesn't support writing essays in place of building.

**What he's done** (not in the vault): PG built Viaweb first and became a prolific essayist only afterwards. His essays then became a major source of YC's applicants and reputation. So for him, writing came after he had built something.

**What would change his answer:** If the writing is how you work out the idea, or how you reach the exact users you're building for, it's part of the work and not a distraction.

**Caveat:** PG is a professional essayist and says of writing "Some of us like it", so he's biased toward valuing it.

**Verdict:** Stay small. Paul Graham would tell you the round is not a reason to hire. If you raise money, rent an office and staff up before users clearly want the product, you are "playing house." He'd hire only when growth forces you to, and only people who are nearly founders.

**Based on:** said it (2014 lecture), plus one essay of his that isn't in the vault, marked below.

**Why he'd say it**
- He names "raise, then hire" as a classic way founders fail: "They raise funding at a nice valuation. They rent a nice office in Soma, hire a bunch of their friends. And then the next step … is gradually realize how completely fucked they are." The cause is that they "neglected the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want." ([Before the Startup, 2014 @ 6:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=417s))
- He also says when to hire: "ideally, you're successful before you even hire two or three people." He points to Airbnb, which took five months to make its first hire. ([@ 34:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2084s))
- He's specific about who to hire first: "the first hires in a startup are almost like founders… You shouldn't have to manage them much." ([@ 34:44–35:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=2118s)) If you need managers to make a hire work, it's too early for that hire.
- In 2024 he went after the standard scaling advice, "hire good people and give them room to do their jobs." He says that in practice it often means "hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground." ([Founder Mode](https://paulgraham.com/foundermode.html))
- **Not in the vault, but a well-known PG position:** in *Default Alive or Default Dead* (2015) he says hiring too fast is the most common way startups die after raising money. More people don't fix a lack of growth, and they shorten your runway. He'd have you check whether you're "default alive" before every hire.

**What YC has done:** Jessica Livingston says YC could move to Silicon Valley within months only because it hadn't hired staff in Cambridge: "start small so you can be nimble and open to change." ([Livingston 2018 @ 25:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1510s)) Garry Tan (2026) pushes the same way from another angle: founders using AI agents reach revenue per employee that never existed before.

**What would change his answer:** clear product-market fit, with growth limited by how many people you have rather than by demand. Even then he'd want each early hire to be a self-motivated peer, chosen the way you'd choose a friend.

**Verdict:** PG would tell you to work on the idea you're passionate about, provided you're trying to build a startup with a big outcome. He also says not to worry about market size at the start. An idea you picked because the market looked big is the kind he says tends to be "bad and plausible sounding."

**Based on:** said it. He wrote about almost exactly this tradeoff in *When To Do What You Love* (2024) and *How to Earn a Billion Dollars* (2026).

**Why he'd say it**
- **For a startup, interest wins. The reason is how big ideas show up, not motivation.** "If you want to make a really huge amount of money — hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars — it turns out to be very useful to work on what interests you the most." He adds: "The reason is not the extra motivation you get from doing this, but that the way to make a really large amount of money is to start a startup" ([When To Do What You Love](https://paulgraham.com/when.html)).
- **Ideas you choose because the market looks good are suspect.** "the best ideas tend to be such outliers that you'd overlook them if you were consciously looking for ways to make money" (same essay). In 2014: "if you make a conscious effort to try and think of startup ideas, you will think of ideas that are not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding" ([How to Start a Startup lecture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s) @ 24:34).
- **Market size today is the wrong number to optimize.** "Don't worry about the second number, the market size. Since you predict future demand, the market will grow." And: "it's always possible to expand into adjacent markets. All you need is a beachhead in the territory of unsatisfied need that you can expand from" ([How to Earn a Billion Dollars](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html)). Seibel and Caldwell back this up: Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe all ended up much bigger than their founders' own estimates.
- **The biggest companies started as projects for fun.** "Many if not most of the biggest startups began as projects the founders were doing for fun. Apple, Google, and Facebook all began that way" ([When To Do What You Love](https://paulgraham.com/when.html)).

**What would change his answer**
- **If your goal is moderate money rather than a startup.** He calls this the "midwit peak": "if your main goal is to make money, you can't usually afford to work on what interests you the most. People pay you for doing what they want, not what you want." In that middle zone, the idea that pays wins.
- **If the "passion" isn't real interest.** He means curiosity about the problem itself, or building something you and your friends actually want. That's what makes it a prediction of future demand. Here's his test for whether the interest is real: "if their work didn't pay well, would they take day jobs doing something else in order to do it in their spare time?"
- **If you can't decide, try both.** "When you can't decide which path to take, it's almost always due to ignorance." His advice is to get more certainty by working on the options, not by thinking harder about them.

One more thing the vault suggests, which is my inference rather than something PG says: he'd probably question the premise. To him a "bigger market" you can see today often means a crowded, obvious idea. The passion project, if it serves a real need, may be the one whose market turns out bigger.

**Verdict:** Apply to YC. Don't put your effort into an angel round. PG would say the real question is whether you're building something people want, because a startup that's growing fast can raise from angels whenever it likes. Since that comes later anyway, take YC's standard deal and batch now and spend the months you'd have spent pitching on growth.

**Verdict:** Paul Graham would tell you not to start alone. He also wouldn't tell you to go looking for a co-founder as a separate task first. In his view the co-founder comes the same way the idea does: you build things with people you already like and respect, and the startup grows out of that work.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has no PG quote that says "solo vs. co-founder" directly. His stance against solo founders is well known, but it comes from essays that aren't in the vault (marked below).

**Why he'd say it**
- **Co-founders come along with the idea.** His recipe for having startup ideas is "1, learn about things that matter. 2, work on problems that interest you. 3, with people you like and respect. ([paulgraham.com/prepare.html](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html), 2026)
- **Choose them the way you'd choose friends, and don't rush it.** "Work with people you genuinely like and respect ... and that you have known long enough to be sure. ([@ 4:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=278s)) In practice that means not picking someone you met last month on a matching site just so you have a co-founder.

His reasons are that a solo founder has no one to keep their morale up, no one to argue ideas with, and investors take it as a sign that nobody you know would join you.

**Other YC voices agree:** Dalton Caldwell (2026) says that "the number one cause of death when you're a founder is it just sort of dies on the vine and you run out of hope and you give up." **What he'd actually have you do:** Start building now and don't wait for a co-founder to appear. Do it alongside people you respect, through side projects, hackathons or a lab. If someone becomes indispensable while you work together, they're your co-founder.

**What would change the answer:** The vault doesn't give a condition under which PG favors going solo. Caldwell says "Not having a co-founder is fine for a lot of people" and that YC has funded solo founders who succeeded. If you do go alone, his condition is that you build co-founder-like relationships around you with early employees, advisors or friends.
